text:
This is why I ask you: the Perfected Person seeks no reputation, so why do you take such pleasure in being known? <margin>This is the conduct of the Perfected Person who does not seek to be known or prominent; why then, Master, do you take such joy in reputation?</margin> Confucius replied, "How excellent!" He then gave up his <margin>He did not value flashiness.</margin> social circles, sent away his disciples, and fled to the great marshes. He wore clothes of coarse fur and hemp, and ate acorns <margin>He did not value rare flavors.</margin> and chestnuts. He entered among the beasts and did not disturb their herds; he entered among the birds and did not disrupt their ranks. <margin>He did not give rise to a mind of discrimination, and thus did not disturb the groups of birds and beasts.</margin> If even birds and beasts did not dread him, how much less would <margin>Even different species did not dislike him.</margin> men?

Confucius asked <term>Zi Sanghu</term> <gloss>The surname and name of a certain recluse</gloss>: "I was twice driven out of Lu, had a tree felled over me in Song, had my footprints erased in Wei, was reduced to poverty in Shang and Zhou, and was besieged between Chen and Cai. Having encountered these many disasters, my kinsmen and old friends have grown increasingly distant, and my followers and associates have increasingly dispersed. Why is this?"

<summary>Confucius adopts the humble life of a recluse in the wilderness to escape the burdens of reputation and questions Zi Sanghu about his repeated political failures and social isolation.</summary>
<keywords>Confucius, Zi Sanghu, Perfected Person, reputation, reclusiveness, political exile, Lu, Song, Wei, Chen, Cai</keywords>
